question: What defines epilepsy as a chronic neurological condition in a patient?

options.A: Having a single febrile convulsion in childhood
options.B: Experiencing two or more unprovoked seizures
options.C: Suffering a seizure caused by severe dehydration
options.D: Fainting due to postural hypotension in the ward

explanation: Epilepsy requires multiple unprovoked seizure events over time for a definitive clinical diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h1)

question: Why is taking a detailed history important when a patient presents with a fit?

options.A: To separate true epileptic seizures from non-epileptic events
options.B: To prevent the family from interfering with ward routines
options.C: To immediately calculate the correct drug dosage needed
options.D: To prove the patient has a permanent psychiatric disorder

explanation: Accurate histories help clinicians rule out mimics like fainting spells or metabolic blackouts before starting treatment. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h1)

question: Which neurotransmitter acts as the primary inhibitory chemical in the brain?
explanation: GABA suppresses neuronal activity, acting as the main brake against excessive brain electrical firing. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h2)

question: What happens at the cellular level during a sudden seizure episode?

options.A: Glucose and oxygen levels in the brain tissue dramatically rise
options.B: GABA production increases to slow down the firing neurons
options.C: Neuronal excitation vastly overwhelms the inhibitory mechanisms
options.D: Brain cells completely stop all electrical and chemical signaling

explanation: A seizure represents a runaway train of electrical signals where excitation beats out suppression. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h2)

question: Which seizure type begins in one specific hemisphere and affects only a localized area?
explanation: Focal seizures originate within neuronal networks limited to one cerebral hemisphere. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is the hallmark behavioral sign of a classic absence seizure in a pediatric patient?

options.A: Uncontrolled wandering around the hospital ward aimlessly
options.B: Violent rhythmic jerking of all four limbs on the floor
options.C: A loud cry followed by immediate stiffening of the body
options.D: A sudden brief blank stare with a temporary lapse in awareness

explanation: Absence seizures feature quick, unnoticeable staring spells without major motor convulsions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is the most frequent cause of breakthrough seizures in patients already diagnosed with epilepsy?
explanation: Failing to take prescribed anticonvulsants leads to subtherapeutic blood levels and provokes seizures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h4)

question: Which tropical infection is a major contributing etiology for secondary seizures in children in Nigeria?
explanation: Severe malaria affecting the brain frequently induces acute symptomatic seizures in endemic zones. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h4)

question: Which diagnostic tool records electrical wave patterns of the brain to help detect seizure activity?
explanation: An EEG measures voltage fluctuations resulting from ionic current within the neurons of the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h5)

question: A patient is admitted after a fit. Why is ordering a blood glucose test an immediate priority?

options.A: Diabetes medications always interfere with brain electrical waves
options.B: Low blood sugar prevents the EEG machine from recording
options.C: High blood sugar causes permanent post-ictal paralysis
options.D: Severe hypoglycemia can directly trigger acute seizure activity

explanation: Metabolic imbalances like low blood glucose are easily reversible triggers for acute fits. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h5)

question: What is the correct immediate nursing action when a patient begins having a tonic-clonic seizure in bed?

options.A: Leave the bedside immediately to find the attending doctor
options.B: Turn the patient onto their side to keep the airway clear
options.C: Force a metal spoon between the teeth to stop tongue biting
options.D: Hold all four limbs down tightly to prevent violent shaking

explanation: The recovery position prevents secretions from pooling in the pharynx and causing aspiration. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h6)

question: Why is forcing objects into a seizing patient's mouth strictly contraindicated in nursing practice?

options.A: It can fracture teeth and obstruct the patient's airway
options.B: It causes the patient to enter a permanent coma state
options.C: It increases the risk of catching a bloodborne infection
options.D: It immediately stops the brain from producing electrical waves

explanation: Trying to pry jaws apart during a forceful tonic contraction damages oral structures and risks suffocation. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary clinical goal of prescribing antiepileptic drugs to a patient with epilepsy?

options.A: To lower blood pressure and improve overall heart rhythm
options.B: To sedate the patient so they sleep through the night
options.C: To permanently cure the underlying brain tissue damage
options.D: To raise the seizure threshold and stabilize neuronal firing

explanation: AEDs work by dampening excessive electrical excitability in the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h7)

question: Why must a nurse warn a patient never to stop taking their antiepileptic drugs abruptly?

options.A: Sudden withdrawal can precipitate life-threatening rebound status epilepticus
options.B: The patient will instantly lose the ability to speak or walk
options.C: Hospital regulations forbid refilling prescriptions after missed doses
options.D: It causes immediate weight gain and severe hair loss overnight

explanation: Abrupt cessation removes the chemical brake holding neuronal hyperactivity in check. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h7)

question: What defines status epilepticus as a medical emergency in clinical practice?

options.A: A continuous seizure lasting longer than five minutes
options.B: A patient experiencing one nocturnal fit per month
options.C: A mild headache occurring after taking anticonvulsant pills
options.D: A single brief absence seizure lasting only three seconds

explanation: Prolonged seizures exceeding five minutes risk permanent brain damage and require immediate rescue protocols. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h8)

question: What is the typical first-line pharmacological treatment administered intravenously during status epilepticus?
explanation: Rapid-acting benzodiazepines quickly suppress continuous electrical discharges to halt status epilepticus. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h8)

question: What safety advice should a nurse give to a young adult newly diagnosed with epilepsy?

options.A: Stop all physical exercise and remain in bed all day long
options.B: Avoid swimming alone and cooking over dangerous open fires
options.C: Only take medications when you feel a headache starting
options.D: Wear a heavy helmet at all times inside the house

explanation: Practical precautions protect patients from drowning or severe burns if an unexpected fit occurs. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h9)

question: Why is addressing social stigma an important part of holistic nursing care for epilepsy patients?

options.A: Negative community attitudes directly alter the electrical wave patterns
options.B: Stigma often leads to treatment default, isolation, and poor health outcomes
options.C: Social isolation cures the underlying brain infection automatically
options.D: Doctors refuse to prescribe drugs to patients facing local gossip

explanation: Fear of discrimination frequently drives patients to hide their condition and abandon necessary therapy. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T11#GNS222_U4_T11_h9)
